1.pericope_label: Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh, and his answer

schools.summary: Gill records that the king's name is variously given as Cenchres or Amenophis, and observes that Pharaoh had never heard the divine name before, taking it perhaps for a deity and perhaps for a king whose ambassadors these were; that it is pronounced here at all he takes as showing the name is not ineffable, whatever the Jews say. Calvin takes the king's retort harder than the rest — that a mortal should so wantonly scorn God is scarcely credible, as though he spat towards heaven — and explains it by Pharaoh's devotion to his own gods, his mockery of an unknown name being meant to display his piety, much as Pilate asked what is truth. Such madness, he adds, may be remarked in all idolaters, who being intoxicated by their errors boldly mock at God and do not deign to inquire about him.

Henry marks a first in the message, and Wesley repeats him almost word for word: in treating with the elders Moses was directed to call God the God of their fathers, but in treating with Pharaoh they call him the God of Israel, and this is the first time in scripture that he is so called of the people rather than of the man — they are just beginning to be formed into a people when God is called their God. Two things follow for both men: they were God's people, and therefore Pharaoh ought not to detain them in bondage; and he expected services and sacrifices from them, and therefore they must have leave to go where they could freely exercise their religion without giving offence to the Egyptians or receiving it from them. Of the reply both hear a flag of defiance hung out by a king summoned to surrender — who is Jehovah? I neither know him nor care for him, neither value nor fear him — and both add the reasoning behind it, that Israel being a despised and oppressed people, Pharaoh estimates their God by the character they bore and concludes that he made no better a figure among the gods than his people did among the nations. Henry alone presses further, that hardened persecutors are more malicious against God himself than against his people, and that here is the core of the whole controversy: God must rule, and man will not be ruled.

Clarke will not read the question as unbelief in general, since Pharaoh spoke under the common persuasion that every place and people had a tutelary deity, and supposed Jehovah might be the tutelary deity of the Israelites, to whom an Egyptian could be under no obligation; it is not judicious, he says, to bring this question as proof that Pharaoh was an atheist, of which the text affords no evidence.

Ellicott places the scene before it begins, since the two men left their usual residence and approached the Court, which the Psalms locate at Zoan, the ordinary seat of Rameses and his son; he notes that the Pharaohs claimed direct communication with their own deities and so could not well deny the possibility of Hebrew leaders communicating with theirs. He also observes that the demand as put was deliberately moderate, God's entire purpose not being revealed at once, so that Pharaoh was tried with a request he might well have granted and showed himself harsh and inconsiderate by refusing. Keil adds that the visit was only preliminary in character, the two making known the will of their God without accrediting themselves by miraculous signs or pressing his demand, since this first step was intended chiefly to show Moses how Pharaoh and the people stood towards the work of God.

debates.question: What does Pharaoh's question reveal about him?

positions.position: not atheism; he assumed every people had a tutelary deity and reckoned he could owe nothing to the Hebrews' God
a wanton scorn of God, an idolater's mockery meant to display piety towards his own gods
the contempt of a hardened persecutor, who estimates the God of Israel by the low condition of Israel

outliers.note: reads the interview as preliminary by design, unaccompanied by signs, and intended to show Moses how both king and people stood towards the work before it began

themes: the God of Israel named for the first time
who is Jehovah, that I should obey his voice
a first demand deliberately moderate

3.pericope_label: The second plea, and the charge of idleness

schools.summary: Gill notes that, perceiving Jehovah was unknown to Pharaoh and treated scornfully, they leave the word out and say only the God of the Hebrews, a people dwelling in his country whom he knew well enough by that name. He observes further that Pharaoh was not struck dumb, whatever Artapanus reported, and that the complaint of the people's numbers cuts both ways, since if some were taken off there were plenty left to work. Calvin hears the threat as reaching the king by inference: if God would take vengeance on a people kept back against their will, how should he escape with impunity who has professedly entered into contention with God? He finds it surprising that a king who took Moses and Aaron for ringleaders did no worse than reprove them and set them to the common labour, and concludes that he was restrained by God, since moderate rigour never satisfies tyrants.

Henry admires the manner of the request, and Wesley repeats him: they make no complaint of the rigour they were ruled with, they plead that the journey was no project formed among themselves but that their God had met with them, and they beg with all submission, we pray thee — for the poor useth entreaties, and though God may summon princes that oppress, it becomes us to beseech and make supplication to them. What they ask is reasonable, only a short vacation, and the reason they give is a good one: lest, if they quite cast off his worship, he fall upon them with one judgment or other, and then Pharaoh will lose his vassals.

Clarke will not let the sacrifice pass as a formality, since great stress is laid on it and no religious act they performed could be acceptable without it; and he explains why it could not be done where they were, the animals they must offer being held sacred by the Egyptians. He quotes Dodd for the tone of the whole speech, that in this first application we observe the proper respectful submission due from subjects to their sovereign, since they represent the danger they themselves would be in by disobeying their God but do not so much as hint at any punishment that would fall on Pharaoh. Of the king's reply he hears an accusation of revolt, with Moses and Aaron charged as ringleaders of sedition — an unprincipled charge, often repeated since, against men who laboured to bring the common people out of ignorance and profligacy to a knowledge of God — and he paraphrases get you to your burdens as let religion alone and mind your work, the language not only of tyranny but of the basest irreligion.

Ellicott reads the second approach as a concession of ground, since Moses accepts Pharaoh's view and does not insist on Jehovah's authority over Egyptians but makes an appeal to pity: he has at any rate authority over Hebrews, and having made a requirement will be angered if they neglect it, so will not Pharaoh let them escape that anger? He gives the second half of the threat a local colour, noting that Egypt lay very open to invasion on its eastern frontier, that the brunt of such an invasion would fall upon the Hebrews, and that under the nineteenth dynasty Hittite incursions were especially feared. Keil says Pharaoh would hear nothing of any worship at all, believing the wish a mere excuse for procuring holidays from labour, and that with a people so numerous he would lose by their keeping any; the phrase he uses for them, the people of the land, Keil takes not as a claim of ownership but as a class name, land-people, that is common people, set against the ruling castes of Egypt.

debates.question: What does the phrase the people of the land mean here?

positions.position: a class name — land-people, that is common people, set against the ruling castes, not a claim that they were the king's property
a complaint of their numbers, which cuts both ways, since if some were taken off there were plenty left to work

outliers.note: quotes Dodd for the deference of the speech, that the two represent only the danger they themselves would run by disobeying their God and never hint at any punishment that might fall on Pharaoh

themes: the God of the Hebrews hath met with us
why the sacrifice could not be offered in Egypt
worship treated as sedition

6.pericope_label: Straw withheld, the tale of bricks unchanged

schools.summary: Gill will not decide what the straw was for, since it may have been mixed with the clay to make the brick firmer or used to burn them; he cites Pococke on the Egyptian pyramid of unburnt brick, made of the Nile's black sandy earth mixed with chopped straw to bind the clay. Calvin reads the two ranks of officials differently from the rest and gives the tyrant credit for cunning, taking both to have been drawn from the children of Israel on the ground that in so great a multitude some might have evaded Egyptians, whereas Israelites set over their own people would know them too familiarly for any to escape. From the increase itself he draws the lesson he thinks it was for, that when God has begun to regard us in order to relieve our troubles he sometimes takes occasion to increase the pressure of our burdens, so that the very engagement to deliver Israel was followed by a heavier bondage; thus it pleases God to prove the faith of his people, and to lift up minds too much set on earth. On the phrase vain words he will not let the king pass as merely politic: in calling the promises vain his impiety bursts out in the middle of his tyranny, and he is instigated to undermine the faith of the Church, since Satan never ceases to employ that same machination against the faithful, as if all that God promises were deceit and vanity.

Clarke distinguishes the ranks by their words: the taskmasters were exactors, men who wrung from the people an unreasonable proportion of labour, and were Egyptians, while the officers were Hebrews, an inferior sort who attended on their superiors to execute orders, something like our sheriffs. He rules out the notion that the straw was for burning, since eastern bricks were clay and straw kneaded together and dried in the sun rather than fired, which Philo confirms when he says straw is the bond by which the brick is held together, and Shaw when he observes that the straw in surviving bricks still keeps its original colour — proof they were never burned. He also notes that the desire to worship the true God is here attributed to an unwillingness to work, a reflection still cast, in principle, upon those who are fervent in spirit serving the Lord and yet not slothful in business. Wesley says the same of the officials in a line, the taskmasters Egyptians and the officers Israelites employed under them.

Ellicott sets out a fuller hierarchy of three grades — lords of service, who settled what works the Hebrews should do; taskmasters beneath them, Egyptians too, serving as intermediaries; and officers, literally scribes, who were Hebrews and kept the tale of the bricks — an arrangement he finds consonant with a governmental system that was bureaucratic and complex. He agrees that crude brick was general in Egypt and always made of Nile mud bound with chopped straw, and measures what the new order cost: Canon Cook reckoned it would more than double their toil, since they must now disperse over harvest fields often lying at a distance, detach the straw from the soil, gather it into bundles and carry it back, and then still complete the ordinary tale. Of the king's last phrase he takes the vain words to be the promises of deliverance by which Moses and Aaron had raised the people's hopes, and hears an echo of Sennacherib dismissing what Hezekiah had spoken. Keil renders the command as let the work be heavy upon the people, that they may stick to it and not look at lying words, and identifies those words as Moses' report that the God of Israel had appeared and demanded a festival.

both drawn from the Israelites, since men set over their own people would know them too well for any to escape

debates.question: What was the straw used for?

10.pericope_label: The people scattered for stubble, the officers beaten

schools.summary: Gill notes what the new order really required, that they were now bidden to fetch the straw themselves and get it where they could, in fields or barns, and adds that if they had to pay for it out of their labour the oppression was greater still. From the fourteenth verse he settles a question the chapter had left open, since the officers are said to be men whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over the people: that shows not only that the two ranks were different persons but that the taskmasters were Egyptians appointed by Pharaoh, while the officers were Israelites set over the poorer sort to render in the tale of bricks. Calvin measures the impossibility of the thing, since to make bricks at all they should have stayed in one place and instead must disperse to gather stubble in the distant parts of Egypt; they could not do both, and that was the point, the order being framed to procure a false pretext which the king might catch at as ground of condemnation. He holds that Pharaoh knew perfectly well the charge of idleness was false, and made it precisely so that the people might turn away from Moses and abandon the hope held out to them from on high; he ordered the officers beaten so that by their punishment the whole people might be in greater dread, and once he had determined to crush them until he had destroyed in them all recollection of God there was no more feeling or pity in him than in a stone.

Henry draws out the several miseries of it — what a wretched thing slavery is, and how valuable liberty and property look to those whose services and possessions lie at the mercy of an arbitrary power; and how strangely God delivers, bringing his people to the utmost straits when he is just ready to appear for them, since the lowest ebbs go before the highest tides and very cloudy mornings commonly introduce the fairest days.

Wesley records the officers' own answer in a line, that if straw had been given them they would have fulfilled their task. Clarke describes the beating itself, probably the bastinado, still the common Egyptian punishment for minor offences: the culprit lies on his belly with his legs turned up behind while the executioner strikes the soles of his feet with a stick — after which the sufferer cannot walk for many weeks, and some are lamed for life.

Keil is exact about what they actually gathered, since the phrase does not mean stubble instead of straw but that they were to collect the stubble left standing in the fields to serve for the chopped straw the bricks required; and he states the arithmetic that made this unanswerable, the quantity being fixed for every day just as when the straw had been given out, so that when the Israelites could not do the work appointed their own overlookers were beaten by the Egyptian bailiffs. Ellicott explains why there was so much stubble, since reaping in Egypt took off the ears only and left a tall stubble which the cultivators did not value and anyone might collect — though having carried it in bundles to the brick-fields they still had to chop it small before it was fit for use. He reports that Egyptian reliefs show foreign labourers at brick-making under overseers armed with sticks, who hasten the workmen whenever they stop to rest and are represented as saying continually, work without faintness; and he adds that the beating of the head men is the usual practice of the East, where a requisition laid on a town is left to those alone answerable to the government, who are punished when they fail to exact it.

debates.question: Why did Pharaoh accuse the people of idleness when he knew they could not meet the tale?

positions.position: to procure a false pretext for condemnation, and so that the people might turn from Moses and abandon the hope held out to them
the officers answered it plainly enough — had straw been given them, the task would have been fulfilled

outliers.note: reads the scene off the monuments, where foreign brick-makers are driven by stick-bearing overseers whose words are recorded as work without faintness

themes: stubble gathered in place of straw
the bastinado and the eastern head man
why the charge of idleness was made

15.pericope_label: The officers appeal to Pharaoh and are called idle

schools.summary: Gill supposes the men came with tears in their eyes and in real hope, little thinking that what they suffered was by Pharaoh's own order; they took it for the taskmasters' doing and expected redress, and were mistaken. Of the answer he notes that instead of showing any indignation at the taskmasters, Pharaoh insulted the men in a flouting, sarcastic way and repeated the charge of idleness twice over, as though its certainty were beyond question; and to the officers in particular he says, go about your business, work yourselves as well as see that your people work, and do not trouble me with such applications.

Henry sees the officers caught between two fires, since they must either abuse the men under them or be abused by the men over them, and thinks it to their credit that rather than tyrannize they would be tyrannized over. Where else, he asks, should they carry a remonstrance of their grievances but to the supreme power, which is ordained for the protection of the injured? Bad as Pharaoh was, his oppressed subjects had liberty to complain to him, and there was no law against petitioning. He calls their representation modest but moving — thy servants are beaten, and yet the fault is in thy own people, the taskmasters, who deny us what is necessary for carrying on our work — and draws from it the observation that it is common for those to be most rigorous in blaming others who are most blameworthy themselves. Of the reply he says that when they were almost killed with working they were told they were idle, and that it is common for the best actions to be mentioned under the worst names; it is well for us that men are not to be our judges, but a God who knows upon what principles we act, so that those diligent in doing sacrifice to the Lord will escape with him the doom of the slothful servant, though with men they do not.

Clarke reads the disputed clause as a charge laid squarely on the Egyptians: the sin is in thine own people, first because they require impossibilities, and second because they punish us for not doing what cannot be performed. Of the taunt he turns the application forward on the reader, since it is common for those unconcerned about their own souls to set down the religious earnestness of others to idleness or a disregard of their secular concerns, and strange that they cannot see there is a middle way, seeing that he who commanded men to be diligent in business commanded them also to be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord.

Ellicott confirms that the access was real, since the Egyptian monarchs were accessible to all and it was part of their duty to hear complaints in person, most of them giving the earlier hours of each day to it, while those who came cried to them for justice after the Oriental fashion. On the disputed clause he says there can be no reasonable doubt that it is set in opposition to the one before it, so that though the Hebrews are punished the people really in fault are the Egyptians; and Keil reaches the same conclusion on grammatical ground, since thy people stands over against thy servants and must therefore mean the Egyptian people rather than the Israelites. Ellicott also shows why the taunt would sting an Egyptian ear, since idleness was reckoned among the worst of sins in Egypt, to be specially disclaimed in the final judgment before Osiris and sometimes disclaimed again in the epitaphs men set on their tombs; he adds that a good deal of idleness did in fact result among the Egyptians themselves from frequent attendance on religious festivals, which may have made the charge seem plausible.

debates.question: Whom does the clause the fault is in thine own people accuse?

positions.position: the Egyptians, who require impossibilities and then punish men for not performing them
the Egyptians, the clause standing in opposition to thy servants and so distinguishing them from the Israelites
the taskmasters, who deny what is necessary for carrying on the work

outliers.note: shows the taunt was worse in Egypt than elsewhere, idleness being a sin disclaimed before Osiris at the judgment and even on tomb epitaphs — while Egyptian religious festivals themselves bred a good deal of it

themes: a right of petition even under Pharaoh
the fault is in thine own people
why idleness was the sharpest charge in Egypt

19.pericope_label: The officers turn on Moses and Aaron

schools.summary: Gill takes the officers' evil case to mean that they could see no likelihood of getting out of it, since not only were the common people in great bondage but they themselves stood to be beaten from time to time for every deficiency. Of their words to Moses he stands between severity and excuse, allowing them to be either a prediction of what would befall Moses and Aaron or an imprecation that God would take notice of their conduct and chastise them for acting the part they had — if not wickedly, yet imprudently. Calvin canvasses the renderings of the phrase and settles on one the others do not consider, that when the officers were forced to publish the king's command their own faces betrayed their sorrow, since they could not evade being the ministers of his cruelty and unwillingly oppressed brethren whose troubles they would rather have lightened; the case was altogether desperate, he concludes, since the very men who carried the edict bore witness by their looks that no mitigation could be hoped for. Of the reproach itself he is severe. It is not wonderful that men so brutalized by the weight of their sorrows should lose all sense of justice, but they are not therefore free from the charge of ingratitude, and we should learn how carefully grief must be restrained, since indulged it parts company with reason and with kindness alike. The root of it he finds in unbelief, because they measured the favour of God by their immediate success: having lately thanked God for the promised redemption they now accuse his messengers as if they had been deceived, and to say the Lord judge is in effect to impose on him the law by which he must condemn himself. Behind it Calvin sees a cowardice natural to almost all of us, who would rather be without God's help than suffer under the cross while he leads us to salvation by a circuitous path.

Wesley, following Henry, marks what the officers ought to have done instead: they should have humbled themselves before God, and rather than that they fly in the face of their best friends — for those called out to public service must expect to be tried not only by the threats of proud enemies but by the unjust and unkind censures of unthinking friends. Clarke states their case shortly, that they saw they could expect neither justice nor mercy, that their deliverance was very doubtful and their case almost hopeless. Of their words he is lenient: these were hasty and unkind expressions, but the afflicted must be allowed the privilege of complaining, since it is all the solace such sorrow can find, and if words are spoken in that distress which cannot be justified, the considerate and benevolent will hear them with indulgence — God is merciful, and the stroke upon this people was heavier even than their groaning.

Ellicott notices that the two were waiting for them, standing in their way to learn the result of the interview, so that the meeting was not sought but could not be avoided; and he adds that the idiom about their savour is common to Hebrew and Egyptian and very expressive, our own being in bad odour with someone running parallel but lacking its force. The sword they speak of he will not dismiss as Oriental hyperbole, since the officers may well have feared that their inability to enforce impracticable demands would end in their own execution. Keil paraphrases the charge closely: they had made the smell of the people stink in Pharaoh's eyes, that is, destroyed their good name with the king and his servants and turned it into hatred and disgust — a pleasant smell being a figure for a good repute, which is why the phrase attaches to the eyes rather than the nose.

not at all; it sprang from unbelief, measuring God's favour by immediate success, and is not free from the charge of ingratitude

22.pericope_label: Moses returns to the Lord and expostulates

schools.summary: Gill reports Bishop Patrick's view that the phrase intimates some settled place where God appeared, to which Moses might resort on all occasions; though Gill himself thinks it may signify no more than that, instead of staying to give the officers an answer he was at a loss to give, he went to God by prayer, as he was wont to do in difficulties. He notes what Moses had expected — that God would make a beginning as soon as the message was delivered, lightening the people's bondage if he did not dismiss them at once — and calls the disappointment a stumbling to him, a temptation to wish he had never been sent. Calvin will not have the expostulation excused. This returning to the Lord he takes in a bad sense, for the forsaking of an office, since Moses is not said to have calmly prayed or humbly sought counsel in a difficulty but to have gone back in disgust to demand his dismissal, as though he had never been sent. He allows that Moses was probably recounting the people's complaints rather than speaking his own mind, yet his bitterness is not altogether excusable when he repents of his vocation; and when he accuses God of slackness it appears how deep the darkness was that had seized his mind, for he had been forewarned that Pharaoh would not yield until crushed by a mighty hand, and now, forgetting it, marvels that the redemption is not already complete.

Wesley, in words Henry had used before him, states the difficulty Moses could not resolve: he knew not how to reconcile the providence with the promise and with the commission he had received — is this God's coming down to deliver Israel? must I, who hoped to be a blessing to them, become a scourge to them? By this attempt to get them out of the pit they are but sunk the further into it. Clarke allows two senses for the returning and prefers the second, since the words may imply a particular place of communing or simply that turning of heart and affection to God which every pious mind is disposed to practise at any time and in any place — a praying heart, as the old adage has it, never lacks a praying place. He renders the last clause literally, delivering thou hast not delivered: thou hast begun the work by giving us counsels and a commission, but thou hast not brought the people out of the hands of their enemies. On the freedom of the complaint he is uncertain and then indulgent, since whether the words are the offspring of a testy impatience and undue familiarity, or of a strong faith which gave Moses more than ordinary access to the throne of his gracious Sovereign, would be difficult to say — but the latter appears the more probable, since the next chapter shows no displeasure at his freedom. He hedges it about all the same: such liberty should never be used but on very special occasions, and then only by God's extraordinary messengers.

Ellicott adds that Moses could find nothing to say to the officers, and that all he could do was complain to God; the freedom of it seems to us almost to border on irreverence, but he holds that God excused it in Moses because it had its root in his tender love for his people.

debates.question: Is Moses' expostulation to be excused?

positions.position: probably yes, as the fruit of a strong faith with unusual access — though such liberty belongs only to God's extraordinary messengers and only on special occasions
yes; the freedom borders on irreverence, but God excused it because it was rooted in tender love for the people
no; it is a forsaking of his office, a going back in disgust to demand dismissal, and it shows how deep the darkness was that had seized his mind

outliers.note: records Bishop Patrick's inference that the phrase implies a fixed place of meeting with God in Egypt, while preferring the plainer reading that Moses simply went to prayer having no answer to give the officers

themes: a praying heart never lacks a praying place
delivering thou hast not delivered
whether Moses may speak so to God
